history_of_present_illness: Paragonimiasis typically presents as chronic bronchitis, characterized by cough and morning expectoration of a gelatinous, usually brownish sputum. It is also known as endemic haemoptysis due to recurrent attacks of varying severity, which may occur after violent exertion or without manifest reason. Symptoms can disappear for months before reappearing. The disease course is very chronic, often lasting many years. Patients are generally well-nourished, but recurrent haemoptysis can lead to marked anaemia. Flukes are usually found in tunnels within the lungs, which are formed by hypertrophied bronchioles with thickened connective tissue walls, and cysts may also form. Beyond lung infection, flukes can invade the brain, liver, and intestines, and wandering flukes may reach other tissues and organs, including the central nervous system, with reported cases of Jacksonian epilepsy linked to ova found in brain cysts.
exposure_and_epidemiology: This infection is caused by the trematode, *Paragonimus westermanni* (also referred to as *P. ringeri* or *Distoma pulmonale*). It is common in parts of Japan and Formosa, with cases also reported in Peruvians who had contact with Japanese immigrants. The life cycle involves eggs in sputum developing into ciliated miracidia in water over several weeks. These miracidia infest certain freshwater molluscs (first intermediate host) where they develop into cercariae. The cercariae then migrate to freshwater crabs (second intermediate host), encysting in their liver or gills. Human infection occurs primarily through eating raw or inadequately cooked infected crabs, such as *Potamon dehaanii* in Japan. After ingestion, the fluke larvae leave their cysts, migrate through the intestine to the abdominal cavity, perforate the diaphragm, enter the pleural cavity, and finally penetrate the lung to encyst. While the lung is the primary site, wandering flukes can invade other tissues and organs, including the central nervous system. Dogs, cats, and especially hogs can also be infected. Prophylactic measures include forbidding the consumption of uncooked crabs or crayfish and sterilizing sputum.
physical_exam: Physical signs on percussion are typically insignificant, but auscultation signs can be marked during episodes of haemoptysis. The adult fluke is flesh-like, covered with scale-like spines, measuring slightly over ⅓ of an inch (8 mm) long. It is almost round in transverse section but has some flattening of the ventral surface. The acetabulum is conspicuous and opens just anterior to the middle of the ventral surface. The branched testicles are located posterior to the laterally placed uterus, and the genital pore opens below the acetabulum. The branched ovary is situated opposite the uterus.
labs_and_diagnostics: Diagnosis of endemic haemoptysis is readily made by identifying the operculated eggs in the sanguinolent sputum. These eggs are light yellow and average 90 × 65 microns in size. Charcot-Leyden crystals are often observed in the sputum. The miracidium stage of the parasite develops from eggs shaken with water. The adult fluke measures a little over 8 mm long, is almost round in transverse section with some flattening of the ventral surface, and possesses a conspicuous acetabulum, branched testicles posterior to the uterus, and a branched ovary.
management_and_clinical_course: The disease typically follows a very chronic course, often lasting many years. Patients usually maintain fair nutrition, though recurrent haemoptysis can lead to significant anaemia. Treatment is entirely symptomatic. Preventive measures include forbidding the consumption of uncooked crabs or crayfish and ensuring the sterilization of sputum to prevent further spread.
